usage: react when something turns out easy
Don't think about it too simply
examples: 이 앱은 기능이 단순해서 쓰기 편해요.
This app is simple in features, so it's easy to use.
단순해서 = 단순하다 + 아서/어서 (reason)
저는 성격이 단순한 편이라 뒤끝이 없어요.
I have a pretty simple personality, so I don't hold grudges.
단순하다 used for an easygoing, uncomplicated personality
문제가 단순하니까 금방 해결될 거예요.
Since the problem is simple, it'll be solved quickly.
단순하니까 = reason; common reassurance
nuance: 단순하다 means simple in structure or design and is usually positive or neutral. Applied to a person it means easygoing and uncomplicated, not stupid. For 'simple = stupid/naive' Koreans say 단순무식하다 or 머리가 단순하다 with extra words.
mistakes: Using 간단하다 and 단순하다 interchangeably; 간단하다 is for quick/brief tasks (간단한 식사), 단순하다 is for plain/uncomplicated structure
Saying 단순한 사람 to mean a dumb person; it actually sounds like an easygoing, low-drama person

english: to be dense, finely-spaced, tightly woven
usage: 촘촘한 + N; teeth set close together
examples: 모기장 구멍이 촘촘해서 벌레가 안 들어와요.
The mosquito net's holes are fine, so bugs can't get in.
촘촘해서 = reason; classic summer-in-Korea use
이 니트는 촘촘하게 짜여서 따뜻해요.
This knit is densely woven, so it's warm.
촘촘하게 짜이다 = to be woven tightly
여행 일정을 너무 촘촘하게 짰더니 힘들었어요.
I packed the travel schedule too tightly, so it was exhausting.
figurative use for an over-packed plan
nuance: 촘촘하다 describes things spaced very closely with tiny gaps: comb teeth, mesh, weaving, stitches, or even a tightly packed schedule. The opposite is 성기다 or 듬성듬성하다 (sparse). It carries a sense of fineness and thoroughness, often positive.
mistakes: Confusing with 빽빽하다; 빽빽하다 stresses crowdedness with no room, 촘촘하다 stresses fine, even spacing
Using it for large objects packed together; 촘촘하다 fits small, repeated units like teeth, threads, dots

examples: 살이 빠져서 청바지가 헐렁해졌어요.
I lost weight, so my jeans got baggy.
헐렁해지다 = to become loose (change of state)
여름엔 헐렁한 옷이 시원해서 좋아요.
In summer, loose clothes are nice because they're cool.
common style preference
문고리가 헐렁해서 곧 빠질 것 같아요.
The door handle is loose, so it looks like it'll fall off soon.
non-clothing use: loose hardware
nuance: 헐렁하다 means loose or baggy, mostly for clothes that don't fit snugly, but also for loosened screws, handles, or fittings. It is the opposite of 꽉 끼다 (too tight) and 빡빡하다 (stiff/tight). For people it can describe a careless, lax attitude (성격이 헐렁하다).
mistakes: Using 넓다 for loose clothes; 넓다 means wide in area, while 헐렁하다 means loose in fit
Forgetting 헐렁해지다 for the change; saying just 헐렁했다 implies it was always baggy, not that it became baggy

english: to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic
usage: the door is stiff (hard to open)
examples: 오늘 회의가 많아서 일정이 빡빡해요.
I have lots of meetings today, so my schedule is packed.
most frequent real-life usage
서랍이 빡빡해서 잘 안 열려요.
The drawer is stiff, so it doesn't open well.
physical sense: tight, resistant
월세 내고 나면 생활비가 빡빡해요.
After paying rent, my living budget is tight.
money sense; relatable for residents
nuance: 빡빡하다 covers two everyday meanings: physically tight/stiff (a drawer or screw that resists moving) and figuratively tight (a packed schedule or a barely-sufficient budget). In both senses it emphasizes having no slack or breathing room. It is colloquial and a touch stronger than 빠듯하다, which leans toward 'just barely enough'.
mistakes: Confusing with 빡세다; 빡세다 (slang) means physically/mentally hard or grueling, while 빡빡하다 means tight with no slack
Using 좁다 for a tight schedule; 좁다 is narrow in space, 빡빡하다 is tight in time/money/resistance

examples: 로션을 발랐더니 피부가 매끄러워졌어요.
After I put on lotion, my skin became smooth.
매끄러워지다 = change of state; ㅂ-irregular
바닥이 매끄러우니까 미끄러지지 않게 조심하세요.
The floor is slick, so be careful not to slip.
매끄러우니까 = reason form
발표가 매끄럽게 끝나서 다행이에요.
I'm relieved the presentation ended smoothly.
figurative: a smooth, polished flow
nuance: 매끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective for surfaces that feel smooth and frictionless: skin, paper, fabric, floors. Figuratively it describes a process or speech that flows without awkward bumps. Note the irregular forms: 매끄러워요, 매끄러운, 매끄러우니까.
mistakes: Conjugating regularly as 매끄럽어요; correct ㅂ-irregular form is 매끄러워요
Confusing with 미끄럽다 (slippery); 매끄럽다 is smooth to the touch, 미끄럽다 emphasizes being slip-prone/dangerous

usage: the way of speaking is harsh
examples: 겨울이라 손이 거칠어져서 핸드크림을 자주 발라요.
It's winter, so my hands get rough and I use hand cream often.
거칠어지다 = becomes rough; seasonal reality
이 수건은 좀 거칠어서 얼굴 닦기엔 별로예요.
This towel is a bit coarse, so it's not great for the face.
texture sense
그 사람은 말투가 거칠지만 마음은 따뜻해요.
That person speaks harshly, but has a warm heart.
figurative: rough manner vs kind nature
nuance: 거칠다 means rough or coarse to the touch (skin, towels, surfaces) and figuratively harsh or rough in manner or speech (말투가 거칠다, 운전이 거칠다). It is the opposite of 매끄럽다/부드럽다. As a ㄹ-stem adjective the ㄹ drops before ㄴ: 거친 손.
mistakes: Writing the modifier as 거칠은; the ㄹ drops, so it is 거친
Limiting it to texture only; 거칠다 also describes harsh speech and aggressive driving (난폭운전)

examples: 음료수를 쏟아서 식탁이 끈적해요.
I spilled a drink, so the table is sticky.
everyday cleanup situation
여름엔 습해서 몸이 끈적해요.
In summer it's humid, so my body feels sticky.
끈적하다 for sweaty, clammy skin
이 로션은 발라도 안 끈적해서 좋아요.
This lotion isn't sticky even after applying, so it's nice.
common cosmetic review point
nuance: 끈적하다 (also 끈적거리다, 끈적이다) describes a sticky, tacky feel: spilled drinks, sweat on humid days, or gooey residue. For Korea's muggy summers it perfectly captures clammy skin. A heavier, syrupy stickiness can be 끈적끈적하다. The opposite clean/dry feel is 보송보송하다.
mistakes: Confusing with 미끄럽다; 끈적하다 grips and clings, 미끄럽다 slides away
Using 달다 (sweet, taste) when you mean the sticky texture; texture is 끈적하다, taste is 달다

english: to be densely packed, crammed, dense
examples: 출근 시간 지하철은 사람이 빽빽해요.
The subway at commute time is packed with people.
very relatable Seoul commute
수첩에 일정이 빽빽하게 적혀 있어요.
The planner is crammed full of appointments.
figurative: a packed schedule written densely
나무가 빽빽해서 햇빛이 잘 안 들어와요.
The trees are dense, so sunlight barely gets in.
nature/forest sense
nuance: 빽빽하다 means crammed full with almost no gaps: a packed subway, a dense forest, tightly written text. It stresses crowdedness and lack of room. Compare 촘촘하다 (fine, even spacing, often positive) and 빡빡하다 (tight schedule/stiff). The opposite is 한산하다 (empty/quiet) or 듬성듬성하다.
mistakes: Confusing with 복잡하다; 복잡하다 means complicated or chaotically busy, 빽빽하다 means physically densely packed
Using 많다 alone for a crowd; 빽빽하다 adds the nuance of being packed with no space

english: to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide
usage: to settle into a roomy spot
examples: 이 카페는 자리가 널찍해서 노트북 하기 좋아요.
This cafe has roomy seating, so it's good for using a laptop.
popular cafe-hunting criterion
원룸치고 화장실이 널찍해요.
For a studio, the bathroom is quite spacious.
house-hunting comment; -치고 = considering
주차장이 널찍해서 주차하기 편해요.
The parking lot is roomy, so parking is easy.
convenience comment
nuance: 널찍하다 means comfortably spacious and roomy, with a positive, pleasant tone. It is a step warmer than plain 넓다 (wide), implying the space feels generous and comfortable. The opposite is 비좁다 (cramped). Great for describing apartments, cafes, and parking when house- or seat-hunting.
mistakes: Using 넓다 when you want the cozy positive nuance; 널찍하다 conveys 'pleasantly roomy', not just measurably wide
Misspelling as 넓직하다; the standard spelling is 널찍하다

english: to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space
usage: feels too small for its purpose
examples: 짐이 많아서 원룸이 너무 비좁아요.
I have a lot of stuff, so the studio feels really cramped.
common renter complaint
엘리베이터가 비좁아서 한 번에 다 못 타요.
The elevator is too cramped, so we can't all fit at once.
everyday building situation
식당이 비좁아서 옆 사람이랑 부딪혔어요.
The restaurant was so cramped I bumped into the person next to me.
tight-space frustration
nuance: 비좁다 means cramped or uncomfortably narrow, stronger and more negative than plain 좁다. The 비- prefix emphasizes that the space is too tight for comfort. It is the direct opposite of 널찍하다. Use it for small rooms, packed elevators, and tight restaurants.
mistakes: Treating 비좁다 as identical to 좁다; 비좁다 adds the nuance of 'too tight to be comfortable'
Using it for a person being narrow-minded; that is 속이 좁다, not 비좁다

examples: 이 운동화는 밑창이 푹신해서 발이 편해요.
These sneakers have a cushiony sole, so my feet are comfortable.
common shoe-shopping comment
호텔 베개가 푹신해서 잘 잤어요.
The hotel pillow was fluffy, so I slept well.
soft-comfort context
새로 산 매트리스가 너무 푹신해서 허리가 좀 아파요.
The new mattress is too soft, so my back hurts a bit.
too-soft can be a downside
nuance: 푹신하다 (often doubled as 푹신푹신하다) describes a soft, springy, cushiony feel: beds, sofas, pillows, shoe soles. It implies pleasant give when pressed. The opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard). For Koreans shopping for furniture or shoes, 푹신하다 is a key comfort word.
mistakes: Confusing with 부드럽다; 부드럽다 is smooth/gentle to the touch, 푹신하다 is springy and cushiony with give
Assuming 푹신하다 is always good; an overly soft (너무 푹신한) mattress can be criticized for back pain

english: to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture
examples: 장마철엔 빨래가 눅눅해서 잘 안 말라요.
During the rainy season, laundry stays damp and won't dry well.
classic Korean monsoon problem
과자 봉지를 안 닫아서 눅눅해졌어요.
I didn't seal the snack bag, so it went soggy.
눅눅해지다 = became soggy
지하라서 그런지 방이 좀 눅눅해요.
Maybe because it's a basement, the room feels a bit damp.
house-hunting red flag
nuance: 눅눅하다 describes things that have absorbed moisture and turned damp or soggy: crackers that lost their crunch, laundry that won't dry, a humid basement room. It is essential vocabulary for Korea's humid summers and 장마 (rainy season). The opposite crisp/dry feel is 바삭하다 or 보송보송하다.
mistakes: Confusing with 축축하다; 축축하다 is wet/moist to the touch (a wet towel), 눅눅하다 is damp-soggy with a stale, humidity-soaked feel
Using 젖다 (to get wet) for soggy snacks; soggy-from-humidity is 눅눅해지다, not 젖다
